​Build in Less than a Day. Showcase on a Global Stage.

​The next generation of AI apps are built on systems that can remember, retrieve context, and take action over real application data. ​Snowflake sits at the exact intersection: the world's data cloud + Cortex Agents + inference next to your data. Agent workflows next to the tables you already have. Token spend visible in the same warehouse you already use for BI.

​TrueFoundry's AI Gateway, Agent Gateway, and MCP Gateway will frame the day. Builders will work on practical agent harness patterns such as model routing, controlled tool access, MCP workflows, observability, eval loops, fallback behavior, budget controls, governance, and deployment paths.

​An agent workflow with model routing, retries, and fallback behavior

​A deployment-minded agent application that shows how it would run inside a real team or platform environment

​Agent systems need to coordinate models, tools, permissions, memory, context, retries, and fallbacks without becoming brittle one-off glue code.

​The Agora Series
An interdisciplinary salon at Apollo Innovation Commons

​In ancient Athens, the agora was never only a marketplace. It was the open ground where the life of the city converged: merchants beside philosophers, citizens beside strangers, commerce and argument unfolding in the same shared space. Ideas did not stay confined to their disciplines. A conversation about geometry might turn toward ethics, and a dispute over trade might surface a question about justice. The agora worked precisely because it refused to keep things apart.

​Something in that arrangement has been lost. Our institutions have grown so specialized that they have become isolated from one another. The biologist and the ethicist, the technologist and the artist, the systems thinker and the practitioner rarely occupy the same room, and more rarely still do they enter into any genuine exchange. Expertise deepens even as the connective tissue between fields grows thin. Yet the problems that matter most, the questions of how we build responsibly, how we care for one another, and how we govern the things we make, tend to live in exactly the spaces between disciplines that our silos are designed to ignore.

​The Agora Series is an attempt to rebuild that common ground. Each gathering draws together voices from across fields, among them frontier technology, the sciences, the arts, philosophy, and civic practice. The aim is not to have them present in parallel but to have them think in company with one another. We have come to believe that the most consequential insights tend to emerge at the edges, where one field presses against another, and that dismantling silos is less a matter of adding panels than of restoring the conditions under which real conversation becomes possible.

​Conversation, though, is only the beginning. The ideas that surface in the Agora do not end when the evening does. They feed directly into the UnCommon Ground Hackathon, our monthly cross-disciplinary build, where the questions raised in dialogue become the raw material for making. Over the course of each gathering, teams drawn from different fields work side by side to prototype, test, and build responses to the problems the Agora brings into focus. It is where thinking together becomes building together. The next UnCommon Ground Hackathon takes place September

​Agora Series #2

​Institutional Transition: The Next Era of Public Goods and Human Capacity

​What was the book, or paper, or poem that expanded your worldview the most?

​Bring it. That is your ticket. You will write one line inside the cover about what it changed, it goes on the shelf with everyone else's, and by the end of the night you leave holding someone else's. Bring a copy you can part with.

​Every era builds the institutions it needs to turn surplus into shared capacity. The library. The research university. The federal agency. The metric. The focused research org. Each one answered the same question in its own vocabulary: what does a society do with abundance, and who gets to decide?

​We are entering an era where a great deal of human capacity gets supported, extended, and in some cases replaced by accelerating technology. Capability is getting cheap. Judgment, trust, meaning, care, taste, and coordination are becoming the scarce goods. No institution we have inherited was built to steward those.

​So we are gathering to ask what nobody currently has a mandate to ask. What does it mean to be human in this era? What do we actually value? What institutions do we need that do not exist yet? And what does the next wave of public goods look like in service of human and planetary flourishing?

​The evening runs as four zones, all open at once.

​The Grounding Bar. Tea poured in slow rounds, cacao, and an elixir bar.

​The Trading Floor. A value exchange, plus a pawn shop where you can hand over a value you have outgrown and walk out with one somebody else surrendered.

​The Bookstore. Every book anyone carried in, shelved with the note they wrote. Six readers on the mic, then open browsing and the exchange.

​Also on the floor: A Salon to discuss our journey of institution-led change, from Carnegie and Rockefeller through the postwar research state, the rights era, the Gates measurement era, and today's focused research orgs and funding mechanisms. Then discussion rounds in small clusters, including the best question we have found so far: what is something society might call a waste of time that has benefited you most?

​We close with the harvest. Everything written on the blocks, the flags, and the ledger, read back to the room.

​A monthly working night for people building embodied AI. No robot required.

​You built the arm at your kitchen table. You trained the policy overnight on your gaming rig. You collected the teleop data in your garage. The one thing none of it came with: labmates.

​Degrees of Freedom is a monthly working night at Mission Robotics for everyone building physical AI without a lab around them. Bring the robot. Bring the sim that refuses to transfer. Bring the gripper that's been 80% assembled since the hackathon. For two hours, the people at the next bench are your labmates.

​Schedule

​6:00 - Kickoff: Who you are, what you're building, what you want working by 9pm.

​6:30-8:30 - Bench time: two hours of real work, quiet enough to think, loud enough to ask the room when you're stuck.

​8:30 - Demos: what moved, or put the problem that's blocking you in front of people who have likely fought it before.

​The person next to you has probably already hit your bug. Robotics failure is multidisciplinary: the fix is rarely in the field you know best. A room of mixed builders is the fastest debugger in the city.

The Next Interface Hackathon: Rethink how we talk to AI
For three years, using AI meant typing into a box and waiting for text to come back.
That era is ending. 

The next interface isn't a chat window. It's worn, spoken, and always on.
Glasses that listen.
A pendant that remembers. 
A tracker you never charge. 
A second self that watches your screen and acts before you ask.
We're putting the founders building that future in one room with the people who want to build on it.

Half a day in San Francisco. 

Real hardware on the table. Working demos, not slideware.
The lineup is a short list of founders shipping the wearables that are pulling AI off the screen. 

The founders in the room:
Adam Cohen Hillel, Secondly - a personal AI "second self" that sees your screen and acts across every app you use. The chat box becomes a presence.
Nik Shevchenko, Omi - the open-source AI wearable necklace, with 250+ developer apps already built on it. Always listening, always yours.
AnhPhu Nguyen, Mira - AI smart glasses with no camera. They hear what you hear, recall every name, and translate 60+ languages in under a second. AnhPhu is the Harvard builder behind last year's viral I-XRAY demo.
Andy Kong, Chargerless - a 7-gram health tracker powered by daylight. One minute of sun a day and it never needs a charger.
What you'll build: pick a device, an API, or a live sensor stream. 

Ship something a person could actually wear or talk to by the time we demo.

 The strongest builds demo to the founders in the room.
This is for builders, hardware hackers, AI engineers, and designers who think the keyboard is a temporary technology.

Auwen Hackathon @ TIAT & Virtual
For all Auwen music producers who have made music with Auwen before. Here is your opportunity to improve your skills, prep for live sets by building up your sound banks, and collaborate with other members of Soniare Collective in multiplayer sessions.
Beginners are welcome if you are ok learning on your own since the focus will be on creating rather than teaching. Other producers and livecoders are also welcome but the emphasis will be on Auwen. This might be your opportunity to experiment with Auwen!
How to join in person
Come to TIAT in SF anytime between 1PM and 9PM. Text Nes if you have trouble getting in. 4067507386
How to Join Virtually
Download the Discord app for desktop if you don't have it yet then go to https://soniare.net/d and join the #hackathon channel. Feel free to join the Discord now or anytime before the event. Make sure to use headphones and test your microphone so you can speak.
Schedule
1 pm - virtual & in-person multiplayer session to make 1 song
3 pm - working on social media profiles and artist presence
4 pm - virtual & in-person multiplayer session to make 1 song
6 pm - working on social media profiles and artist presence
7 pm - solo time building up sound banks for live sets (virtual & in-person)
9 pm - taking turns practicing live sets (virtual & in-person)
11 pm - dinner at Thai place
Food & drink
Some healthy snacks from Jagalchi (a Korean grocery store) will be provided such as sweet potatoes, mochi, and sushi. We can also order food as needed. Some drinks will be provided but also bring a refillable bottle for water.
Donations
Donations are optional but if you want snacks please donate then I'll know to grab some for you. If you can't afford to donate please come for free! Just RSVP to make it more legit so you can get updates from the Luma blasts.
RSVP ahead of time
Please sign up sooner rather than later.
About the host
Nes Croft is a musician, artist, and computer engineer from Montana who has written and recorded thousands of songs since a young age starting with folk/rock as a teenager and expanding into experimental pop, IDM, techno, and trance. Nes gained an interest in electronics at age 19 after working at the DIY synth company Synthrotek in Portland, OR. Going on to earn a bachelor's degree in computer engineering at Montana State University. While in college Nes co-founded and developed Vaytricks Beat Machine, a mobile drum machine app that received over 100,000 downloads. 5 years later Nes left Vaytricks to pursue a live performance focused approach to music production and Auwen was born. Auwen is a digital audio workstation featuring a hybrid producer/DJ workflow that allows musicians to perform dance music live using a command line interface. Given the nature of the software, Nes naturally gravitated toward live music events testing Auwen at various electronic music festivals in Montana. Later, Nes joined the livecoding scene in San Francisco and started hosting workshops & live music events at TIAT art gallery and Gray Area in San Francisco in 2025-2026.
